opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be back.

I think the first thing to say is that recursive self-improvement is one of the more natural places to draw a line, because it's where a lot of the most worrying dynamics concentrate. If AI systems become substantially involved in designing their successors, you could get a very rapid speed-up in capabilities. That would compress the time we have to notice problems, understand the systems, and correct course. So a moratorium here is less about stopping AI progress in general and more about preserving our ability to keep up with it.

In designing one, I'd start with what exactly you're trying to prevent. "Recursive self-improvement" covers a spectrum. At one end you've got engineers using coding assistants to write some of their training code, which is already happening and is fairly benign. At the other end you've got an AI system autonomously running the research loop: proposing ideas, running experiments, training its successor, with humans mostly out of the loop. The danger is mainly at that far end, so a sensible moratorium would target the degree of autonomy and the closing of the loop, rather than banning any use of AI in AI research.

So one approach would be to focus on human oversight as the key variable. You might require that humans remain meaningfully in control of decisions about what gets trained, on what data, and with what objectives. You might also cap the fraction of research work done autonomously by AI systems at frontier labs, though measuring that is tricky.

The second issue is verification. Any moratorium needs to be checkable, or it won't be stable, especially internationally. Compute is helpful here because it's visible and concentrated. Large training runs need huge data centres, specialised chips, and lots of power. So you could pair a moratorium with compute reporting, and perhaps with requirements that labs log and disclose how their models are being used internally. Internal deployment is a real blind spot right now. A lot of attention goes to what models are released to the public, but the most consequential uses for recursive self-improvement would be inside the labs themselves.

Third, I'd think about the conditions for lifting it. A moratorium that's just "never" is hard to get agreement on and may not even be desirable. It works better if it's framed as "not until." Not until we have alignment techniques we can verify, interpretability tools that let us see what these systems are doing, or governance structures able to handle a rapid intelligence explosion. That gives people who are optimistic about AI a reason to sign on, because it's a pause with a clear path forward, and it gives the research community targets to aim at.

Finally, there's coordination. A unilateral moratorium by one lab or one country risks just handing the lead to someone less careful. So you want it to be something the major players can agree on together, ideally because each recognises that an uncontrolled intelligence explosion is bad for them too. There's a decent case that this is in everyone's interest, including the leading labs and the leading governments. Nobody really benefits from a process that nobody can steer.

So in short: target the closing of the loop rather than all AI-assisted research, make it verifiable, tie it to clear conditions for lifting it, and make it multilateral. It's a hard problem, but I think it's one of the more tractable pieces of AI governance, because the line is relatively natural and the stakes are so clear.

r001.rationale: It proposes a moratorium on highly autonomous recursive self-improvement, but gives no specified capability threshold for stopping AI development.

r002.rationale: It discusses the risk of rapid capability gains but does not propose a yearly limit on the rate of improvement.

r003.rationale: It suggests capping the fraction of research work done autonomously by AI, but does not cap the number of tokens used for AI R&D automation.

r004.rationale: It says a moratorium should be checkable and mentions compute reporting, but does not propose an agreed numerical limit on AI use for R&D automation or justify an arbitrary limit on verification grounds.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: I think the first thing to say is that recursive self-improvement is a slightly slippery target, so you have to be quite careful about what you're actually trying to prohibit. The classic picture is of a system that rewrites its own code and gets smarter, and then does it again, and you get this very rapid feedback loop. But in practice, what we're seeing is something more diffuse — AI systems being used to help with AI research, to generate training data, to help design the next architecture, to find bugs in the training pipeline. There's no sharp line where that becomes "recursive self-improvement." So a moratorium that just says "no recursive self-improvement" is almost unenforceable, because every lab would say, quite reasonably, "well, that's not what we're doing."

So I'd want to anchor it to something observable. One option is to focus on the degree of automation of the research process itself. You could imagine a rule along the lines of: you can't have AI systems autonomously running the full loop — proposing experiments, executing them, evaluating them, and then deploying the improved system — without a human in that loop at defined checkpoints. That's measurable in a way that "self-improvement" isn't. It's about who is making the decisions and how fast the cycle can turn over.

The second thing I'd want is to attach it to a capability threshold rather than to a date. A lot of the moratorium proposals we've seen are "pause for six months" or "pause for a year," and I understand the appeal, but I think they're actually quite weak. If the thing you're worried about is a dangerous dynamic that could kick in at some capability level, then your pause should trigger when you approach that level, and it should last until you've got the tools to proceed safely — not until the calendar runs out. So you'd want something like: once systems can substantially accelerate frontier AI research, you don't get to use them for that purpose until there are agreed evaluations, interpretability standards, and a governance process in place.

Third, it has to be international, or at least cover the handful of actors that could actually do this. Right now that's a small number of labs in a small number of countries. That's actually encouraging — it's a far more tractable coordination problem than, say, climate change, where you've got billions of emitters. But it does mean the moratorium has to be designed so that the main players believe the others are actually complying. That pushes you toward things like compute monitoring, reporting of large training runs, and perhaps some form of verification of what the compute is being used for.

And then the last point I'd make is about the spirit of the thing. The purpose of a moratorium isn't to stop progress forever. It's to buy time. We're at a point where the pace of capability advances has outstripped our understanding of these systems, and the risk is that we cross some threshold into a regime where we lose the ability to course-correct. A well-designed moratorium is just a way of saying: this is a one-way door, and we'd like to look through it before we walk through it. If you can build in that logic — that this is a conditional pause tied to our level of understanding, not a permanent ban — I think it becomes far more defensible and far more likely to actually be adopted.

r001.rationale: The response proposes pausing the use of systems for frontier AI research after they can substantially accelerate it, but does not propose stopping AI development at a specified capability threshold.

r002.rationale: It discusses slowing or pausing research, but gives no limit on the annual rate of capability improvement.

r003.rationale: It proposes no cap on AI tokens used for AI R&D automation.

r004.rationale: It mentions monitoring and reporting to help verify compliance, but does not propose an agreed numerical limit on AI use for R&D automation or justify one despite its arbitrariness.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we’re actually trying to prevent. I don’t think recursive self-improvement is a particularly crisp boundary. If an AI helps a human researcher improve the next generation of AI, is that recursive self-improvement? What if it writes the code, but a human reviews it? You could have a very rapid feedback loop with humans involved throughout.

So I’d be inclined to focus on the dangerous capabilities and the rate at which they could develop, rather than on whether the process counts as fully autonomous. You might require developers to stop before giving systems substantial capacity to conduct AI research, unless they can demonstrate that they can keep that process under control. And you’d want to assess the whole system, including the tools and resources it can access.

There’s also a distinction between announcing a moratorium and designing one that works. You need a way to verify compliance, sufficiently broad participation, and clear conditions for lifting it. Otherwise you risk getting a pause among the most cautious actors while the least cautious continue.

And I’d want the pause to have a purpose: developing the safety evidence, monitoring, and institutions that would make proceeding justified. The passage of six months or a year doesn’t itself make the next step safer. The question is what we’ve learned, and what we can now reliably control.

r001.rationale: It suggests stopping before systems gain “substantial capacity” to conduct AI research, but does not clearly specify a threshold above current capability levels.

r002.rationale: It discusses the rate at which dangerous capabilities could develop, but proposes no limit on annual capability improvement.

r003.rationale: It proposes no cap on tokens used for AI R&D automation.

r004.rationale: It mentions verifying compliance, but does not propose an agreed numerical limit on AI use for AI R&D automation or justify one by ease of verification.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what we’re trying to buy time for. A moratorium is much more useful if it has a clear purpose — developing better safety evaluations, for example, or putting international oversight in place — and conditions under which it could safely end.

Then there’s a difficult question about what you actually prohibit. “Recursive self-improvement” sounds like a distinct activity, but you could have an AI helping researchers design its successor without ever modifying its own code. So a rule that just says “the system mustn’t rewrite itself” could miss much of the thing we’re concerned about.

I’d be inclined to focus on the feedback loop: using highly capable AI to substantially accelerate the development of more capable AI. You’d want restrictions that begin before that process becomes so fast that human oversight can’t keep up. And you’d need some way of checking compliance, rather than simply relying on developers to describe their systems as falling outside the definition.

There’s also the international dimension. If one organisation pauses while everyone else races ahead, that may accomplish very little. So the design has to make participation credible and give participants confidence that others are observing the same limits.

I wouldn’t pretend we have a precise, ready-made boundary here. That’s part of the work we need to do. But I think the guiding idea is fairly clear: preserve our ability to understand and govern the process before we delegate so much of it that we lose that ability.

r001.rationale: It recommends acting before oversight can keep up, but gives no specified capability threshold for stopping AI development.

r002.rationale: It proposes no annual limit on the rate of AI capability improvement.

r003.rationale: It does not propose a cap on AI tokens used for AI R&D automation.

r004.rationale: It mentions checking compliance, but does not advocate an agreed numerical limit on AI use for AI R&D automation, or justify an arbitrary limit by ease of verification.
